claim: Non-muscle myosin II motor activity determines the rate of tissue folding in Drosophila.
source: in vivo constriction rate scales with myosin motor activity
evidence: The abstract states this as a main finding, supported by combined biochemical and in vivo measurements.

claim: Phosphomimetic mutants of the Drosophila regulatory light chain (RLC) do not mimic the phosphorylated RLC state in vitro.
source: We show that so-called phosphomimetic mutants of the Drosophila regulatory light chain (RLC) do not mimic the phosphorylated RLC state in vitro.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by biochemical assays showing reduced motor activity compared to phosphorylated RLC-TS.

claim: Tissue recoil following laser ablation is decreased in phosphomimetic mutants compared to wild-type tissue.
source: The defect in the myosin motor activity in these mutants is evident in developing Drosophila embryos where tissue recoil following laser ablation is decreased compared to wild-type tissue.
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated by laser ablation experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Myosin activity is required for rapid cell contraction and tissue folding in developing Drosophila embryos.
source: Overall, our data highlights that myosin activity is required for rapid cell contraction and tissue folding in developing Drosophila embryos.
evidence: Conclusion stated in abstract, supported by correlation between motor activity and constriction rates.

claim: The myosin motor domain catalyzes the hydrolysis of ATP to power the translocation of actin filaments.
source: The motor domain catalyzes the hydrolysis of ATP to power the translocation of actin filaments, a function referred to as motor activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myosin function stated in the introduction.

claim: Phosphorylation of the RLC at conserved Serine and Threonine sites activates myosin motor activity in smooth muscle and mammalian non-muscle myosin.
source: Work done using smooth muscle myosin and mammalian non-muscle myosin have demonstrated that phosphorylation of the RLC at conserved Serine and Threonine sites (Figure 1B, Serine-19 and Threonine-18) activates myosin motor activity, enhances the affinity of myosin for actin, and promotes myosin filament assembly (Heissler and Sellers, 2016).
evidence: Cited from prior literature on mammalian myosins.

claim: Myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK), and Citron kinase activate myosin through direct phosphorylation of the RLC, primarily on Serine-19.
source: Myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK), and Citron kinase are known to activate myosin through direct phosphorylation of the RLC, primarily on Serine-19 (Amano et al., 1996; Heissler and Sellers, 2014; Pearson et al., 1984; Yamashiro et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior studies on myosin regulation.

claim: The importance of myosin light chain phosphorylation in Drosophila has been shown through genetic studies.
source: In Drosophila, the importance of myosin light chain phosphorylation has been shown through genetic studies (Jordan and Karess, 1997; Lee and Treisman, 2004; Mizuno et al., 2002; Ong et al., 2010; Winter et al., 2001).
evidence: Multiple citations to prior genetic studies in Drosophila.

claim: It has not been biochemically demonstrated that Drosophila myosin motor activity and filament assembly is regulated by RLC phosphorylation prior to this study.
source: However, it has not been biochemically demonstrated that Drosophila myosin motor activity and filament assembly is regulated by RLC phosphorylation or whether the extent of activation is similar to that of mammalian systems.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Myosin motor activity may not be essential for actin network contraction in some cases, with myosin functioning mainly as an actin filament crosslinker.
source: Recent evidence has suggested that myosin motor activity is not essential for actin network contraction in some cases, but that myosin's main role is to function as an actin filament crosslinker (Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from prior study suggesting alternative mechanism.

claim: Actin filament crosslinking could drive contraction in the absence of motor activity if linked to actin network disassembly.
source: Actin filament crosslinking could drive contraction in the absence of motor activity, if linked to actin network disassembly (Sun et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited hypothesis from prior study.

claim: Myosin motor activity is not required for apical constriction in epithelial cells of the neural tube, with actin depolymerization being required instead.
source: It was suggested that myosin motor activity is not required for apical constriction in epithelial cells of the neural tube, but that instead actin depolymerization was required for epithelial folding (Escuin et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited claim from prior study that this paper challenges.

claim: Apical constriction during Drosophila dorsal closure results from cell volume reduction rather than myosin motor activity.
source: In addition, it was recently suggested that apical constriction during Drosophila dorsal closure results from cell volume reduction as opposed to myosin motor activity (Saias et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited claim from prior study that this paper challenges.

claim: The ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 disrupts myosin filament assembly, motor activity, and prevents the motor domain from transitioning to the strong actin binding state by blocking RLC phosphorylation.
source: The ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (Uehata et al., 1997) disrupts myosin filament assembly, motor activity, and prevents the motor domain from transitioning to the strong actin binding state by blocking RLC phosphorylation (Sellers et al., 1982).
evidence: Cited effects of ROCK inhibitor from prior studies.

claim: Treatment with a ROCK inhibitor often disrupts myosin localization.
source: Furthermore, treatment with a ROCK inhibitor often disrupts myosin localization (Hirose et al., 1998; Royou et al., 2002; Totsukawa et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited effect from multiple prior studies.

claim: The myosin inhibitor blebbistatin locks the motor domain in a weak actin binding state.
source: The myosin inhibitor blebbistatin locks the motor domain in a weak actin binding state, a state with similar affinity to actin as that of myosin bound to an unphosphorylated RLC (Kovács et al., 2004a; Ramamurthy et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited mechanism of blebbistatin from prior studies.

claim: RLC mutants thought to mimic the activated state of myosin enable some rock mutant flies to survive to adulthood.
source: While RLC mutants thought to mimic the activated state of myosin have been observed to enable some rock mutant flies to survive to adulthood (Winter et al., 2001), studies directly visualizing cell contractility determined that RLC mutants fail to suppress ROCK mutants (Aranjuez et al., 2016; Kasza et al., 2014; Vasquez et al., 2014) or ROCK inhibition (Munjal et al., 2015), questioning whether these mutants truly mimic the phosphorylated state.
evidence: Cited conflicting results from prior studies.

claim: Overexpression of a myosin heavy chain mutant that lacks the motor domain demonstrated the importance of myosin for force generation during morphogenesis.
source: Overexpression of a myosin heavy chain mutant that lacks the motor domain demonstrated the importance of myosin for force generation during morphogenesis; however, this approach would disrupt both motor and crosslinking functions (Franke et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited result from prior study with noted limitation.

claim: The basal ATP hydrolysis rate of RLC-TS in the absence of actin is approximately 0.01 s⁻¹.
source: The basal ATP hydrolysis rate (kbasal) in the absence of actin was ~0.01 s−1 for RLC-TS, which is comparable to the rates of mammalian myosin isoforms (Table 1) (Kim et al., 2005; Kovács et al., 2004b).
evidence: Measured value from biochemical assays reported in the results.

claim: Actin marginally activated the ATP hydrolysis rate of RLC-TS in the absence of RLC phosphorylation.
source: Actin marginally activated the ATP hydrolysis rate of RLC-TS in the absence of RLC phosphorylation.
evidence: Observed result from biochemical assays.

claim: RLC phosphorylation activated myosin motor activity to a maximum ATP hydrolysis rate (kcat) of 1.23 ± 0.07 s⁻¹ with an apparent actin affinity (Kapp) of 38.9 ± 7.32 µM.
source: RLC phosphorylation potently activated myosin motor activity to a maximum ATP hydrolysis rate (kcat) of 1.23 ± 0.07 s−1 with an apparent actin affinity (Kapp) of 38.9 ± 7.32 µM (Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Measured values from biochemical assays reported in results.

claim: Drosophila myosin is regulated by RLC phosphorylation.
source: This result demonstrates that Drosophila myosin is regulated by RLC phosphorylation and that the effect of RLC phosphorylation in Drosophila is quantitatively similar to myosins from higher eukaryotes (Heissler and Manstein, 2013).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from biochemical data showing activation by phosphorylation.

claim: RLC-AS and RLC-TA can each be phosphorylated by MLCK at only one site, either Serine-21 or Threonine-20, respectively.
source: We found that RLC-AS and RLC-TA can each be phosphorylated by MLCK at only one site, either Serine-21 or Threonine-20, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by HPLC-mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: RLC-AA, RLC-AE, and RLC-EE were all unresponsive to MLCK treatment.
source: RLC-AA, RLC-AE, and RLC-EE were all unresponsive to MLCK treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by HPLC-mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: All RLC mutants have a low basal ATP hydrolysis rate of approximately 0.01–0.02 s⁻¹.
source: Similar to RLC-TS, all RLC mutants have a low kbasal of ~0.01–0.02 s−1 (Table 2).
evidence: Measured values from biochemical assays.

claim: MLCK phosphorylation of RLC-AS increased its ATP hydrolysis rate to the same extent as that of the wild type RLC-TS.
source: MLCK phosphorylation of RLC-AS increased its ATP hydrolysis rate to the same extent as that of the wild type RLC-TS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Comparison of biochemical assay results between mutants.

claim: Phosphorylation of RLC-TA activated the ATP hydrolysis rate to a reduced extent compared to RLC-TS.
source: In contrast, phosphorylation of RLC-TA activated the ATP hydrolysis rate to a reduced extent (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, and Table 2).
evidence: Comparison of biochemical assay results.

claim: Serine-21 is the primary RLC phosphorylation site and Threonine-20 is the secondary phosphorylation site in Drosophila myosin.
source: The virtually identical steady-state ATP hydrolysis rates for RLC-TS and RLC-AS at 100 µM actin, but reduced activity of RLC-TA indicate that Serine-21 is the primary RLC phosphorylation site and that Threonine-20 is the secondary phosphorylation site.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ATP hydrolysis rates of different mutants.

claim: Phosphorylation results in approximately 6–7 fold activation for RLC-TS and RLC-AS versus approximately 3 fold activation for RLC-TA.
source: The direct comparison of the ATP hydrolysis rates of RLC-TS and RLC mutants at 100 µM actin (k100), the highest actin concentration used in the assay, shows that phosphorylation results in a ~6–7 fold activation for RLC-TS and RLC-AS versus a ~3 fold activation for RLC-TA, respectively (Figure 1C and Table 2).
evidence: Calculated from biochemical assay data.

claim: RLC-AE and RLC-EE display motor activity that is only 27–28% of the motor activity of phosphorylated RLC-TS.
source: Surprisingly, RLC-AE and RLC-EE display a k100 that was similar to that of RLC-AA and only 27–28% of the motor activity of phosphorylated RLC-TS (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F, Table 2).
evidence: Calculated from biochemical assay data.

claim: Neither RLC-AE nor RLC-EE successfully mimic RLC phosphorylation at Serine-21.
source: This result demonstrates that neither RLC-AE nor RLC-EE successfully mimic RLC phosphorylation at Serine-21.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of motor activities.

claim: No significant movement was detected for RLC-TS in the absence of phosphorylation in the in vitro motility assay.
source: No significant movement was detected for RLC-TS in the absence of phosphorylation, consistent with myosin being in an inactive, weak actin-binding state.
evidence: Result from in vitro motility assay.

claim: Phosphorylation of RLC-TS by MLCK resulted in movement of actin filaments at approximately 250 nm s⁻¹.
source: Phosphorylation of RLC-TS by MLCK resulted in movement of actin filaments at ~250 nm s−1, which is slightly higher than that of human myosin IIA (Figure 1D and Table 3) (Cuda et al., 1997).
evidence: Measured value from in vitro motility assay.

claim: No obvious directed actin filament movement was observed for RLC-AA in the in vitro motility assay.
source: No obvious directed actin filament movement was observed for RLC-AA, consistent with this mutant mimicking the unphosphorylated RLC state.
evidence: Result from in vitro motility assay.

claim: Phosphorylated RLC-AS moved actin filaments at 50% of the rate of phosphorylated RLC-TS.
source: Phosphorylated RLC-AS moved actin filaments at 50% of the rate of phosphorylated RLC-TS and phosphorylated RLC-TA moved actin filaments at only 10% of the rate of phosphorylated RLC-TS.
evidence: Measured values from in vitro motility assay.

claim: Phosphorylated RLC-TA moved actin filaments at only 10% of the rate of phosphorylated RLC-TS.
source: Phosphorylated RLC-AS moved actin filaments at 50% of the rate of phosphorylated RLC-TS and phosphorylated RLC-TA moved actin filaments at only 10% of the rate of phosphorylated RLC-TS.
evidence: Measured values from in vitro motility assay.

claim: RLC-AE and RLC-EE translocated actin filaments at about 30% of the speed of phosphorylated RLC-TS.
source: Both, RLC-AE and RLC-EE translocated actin filaments, demonstrating that these mutants exhibit some level of constitutive functional activity; however, translocation speeds of actin filaments by RLC-AE and RLC-EE were only about 30% of that of phosphorylated RLC-TS, indicating a functional deficit for these mutants (Figure 1D).
evidence: Measured values from in vitro motility assay.

claim: Unphosphorylated RLC-TS and RLC-AA tethered actin filaments to the surface in the in vitro motility assay.
source: Though neither unphosphorylated RLC-TS nor RLC-AA translocated actin filaments in the in vitro motility assay, both motors tethered actin filaments to the surface indicating that unphosphorylated Drosophila myosin still binds actin weakly as occurs with mammalian unphosphorylated myosins, suggesting that bipolar filaments containing these myosins could cross-link or tether actin filaments (Cuda et al., 1997).
evidence: Observation from in vitro motility assay.

claim: RLC-TS and RLC mutants form small bipolar filaments with a length of 312 ± 25 nm and a width of 7.4 ± 1.3 nm that consist of 12.8 ± 4.5 myosin molecules.
source: Electron micrographs show that RLC-TS and RLC mutants form small bipolar filaments, with a length of 312 ± 25 nm and a width of 7.4 ± 1.3 nm that consist of 12.8 ± 4.5 myosin molecules (Figure 2).
evidence: Measured from electron microscopy images.

claim: The appearance of Drosophila myosin filaments is similar to rotary shadowed images of myosin purified from Drosophila cells and those formed by mammalian myosin IIC.
source: The appearance of the filaments is similar to the rotary shadowed images of myosin purified from Drosophila cells and those formed by mammalian myosin IIC (Table 3) (Billington et al., 2013; Kiehart and Feghali, 1986).
evidence: Comparison with cited prior studies.

claim: Full-length RLC-TS is in a two-state equilibrium involving a compact folded (10S) conformation and assembled filaments.
source: We also revealed that full-length RLC-TS is in a two-state equilibrium, which involves a compact folded (10S) conformation and assembled filaments.
evidence: Observed from electron microscopy experiments.

claim: The equilibrium of RLC-TS is shifted from the filamentous form to the 10S conformation in the presence of ATP when the RLC is not phosphorylated.
source: The equilibrium is shifted from the filamentous form to the 10S conformation in the presence of ATP when the RLC is not phosphorylated (Figure 2).
evidence: Observed from electron microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: All RLC mutants form filaments in the absence of ATP and disassemble into the 10S conformation in the presence of ATP.
source: Similar to RLC-TS, all RLC mutants form filaments in the absence of ATP and disassemble into the 10S conformation in the presence of ATP (Figure 2).
evidence: Observed from electron microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Phosphorylated RLC-TS remains predominantly filamentous in the presence of ATP.
source: As occurs with mammalian myosin II paralogs, phosphorylated RLC-TS remains predominantly filamentous in the presence of ATP demonstrating a dual effect of phosphorylation; activation of the ATPase activity and stabilization of the filament structure (28).
evidence: Observed from electron microscopy experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation stabilizes filaments of RLC-AS and RLC-TA in the presence of ATP.
source: Phosphorylation also stabilizes filaments of RLC-AS and RLC-TA in the presence of ATP.
evidence: Observed from electron microscopy experiments.

claim: Addition of ATP to RLC-AA, RLC-AE and RLC-EE results in depolymerization of the myosin filaments.
source: If RLC-AE and RLC-EE were faithfully mimicking the phosphorylated RLC state, they should also remain predominantly filamentous in ATP in vitro at these protein concentrations; instead, addition of ATP to RLC-AA, RLC-AE and RLC-EE results in depolymerization of the myosin filaments.
evidence: Observed from electron microscopy experiments.

claim: The concentration of myosin in Drosophila cells is on the order of 0.5 µM.
source: The concentration of myosin in Drosophila cells is on the order of 0.5 µM, which favors the filamentous form and thus making it likely that all RLC mutants form filaments in vivo (Kiehart and Feghali, 1986; Vasquez et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior studies.

claim: The final apical myosin intensity in folding tissues was similar between RLC-TS and RLC mutant embryos.
source: Using this method, we demonstrated that the final apical myosin intensity in folding tissues was similar between RLC-TS and RLC mutant embryos (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Measured from side-by-side imaging experiments shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Neither full myosin motor activity nor targeted phosphorylation is required for apical myosin localization.
source: These side-by-side comparisons of apical myosin levels, and our previous results where we showed that the RLC-AA mutant localized apically (23), demonstrate that neither full myosin motor activity nor targeted phosphorylation is required for apical myosin localization.
evidence: Inferred from imaging data and prior results.

claim: Tissues expressing either RLC-TA or RLC-AE display lower initial recoil velocities than RLC-TS tissues after laser ablation.
source: We calculated the initial recoil velocity (see Materials and methods) and found that tissues expressing either RLC-TA or RLC-AE display lower initial recoil velocities than RLC-TS tissues, suggesting that RLC mutant tissues generate less tension than RLC-TS tissues (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Calculated from laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Differences between the power law exponents of RLC-TS, RLC-TA, and RLC-AE embryos were not significant.
source: Differences between the power law exponents of RLC-TS, RLC-TA, and RLC-AE embryos were not significant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of laser ablation data.

claim: Differences between time decay constants of RLC-TS, RLC-TA, and RLC-AE embryos were not significant.
source: In agreement with power law exponents, differences between time decay constants of RLC-TS, RLC-TA, and RLC-AE embryos were not significant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of laser ablation data.

claim: Myosin motor activity is important to generate epithelial tension during ventral furrow formation.
source: We conclude that myosin motor activity is important to generate epithelial tension during ventral furrow formation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from laser ablation experiments showing reduced recoil in mutants.

claim: The mean constriction rate for cells in RLC-AS was 74% of that of RLC-TS cells.
source: We found that the mean constriction rate for cells in RLC-AS was 74% of that of RLC-TS cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Calculated from time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cells expressing RLC-TA or RLC-AE constricted with mean rates that were 60% and 47% of RLC-TS cells, respectively.
source: We found that cells expressing RLC-TA or RLC-AE constricted with mean rates that were 60% and 47% of RLC-TS cells, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: Calculated from time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a relationship between myosin motor activity and constriction rate.
source: Taking our in vivo and in vitro measurements of myosin activity, there is a relationship between myosin motor activity and constriction rate (Figure 4B).
evidence: Correlation shown in Figure 4B between in vitro ATPase activity and in vivo constriction rate.

claim: The RLC-AE mutant exhibited the slowest tissue folding behavior, with minimal folding occurring even 9 min after myosin first appeared.
source: The RLC-AE mutant, which had the greatest defect in motor activity, exhibited the slowest tissue folding behavior, with minimal folding occurring even 9 min after myosin first appeared (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The RLC-AS and RLC-TA mutants exhibited tissue folding at intermediate rates, folding over but failing to seal after 9 min.
source: The RLC-AS and RLC-TA mutants exhibited tissue folding at intermediate rates, folding over, but failing to seal after 9 min, a time in which RLC-TS is fully sealed (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The apical constriction rate and tissue folding rate scales with the myosin motor activity.
source: Overall, our results show that the apical constriction rate and tissue folding rate scales with the myosin motor activity.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on correlation between in vitro motor activity and in vivo constriction/folding rates.

claim: Drosophila myosin is insensitive to blebbistatin.
source: Drosophila myosin is insensitive to blebbistatin, a widely-used myosin inhibitor (Heissler et al., 2015; Straight et al., 2003), which has limited tests of in vivo myosin function to genetic disruptions or dominant negative approaches that do not specifically disrupt motor activity (Franke et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from prior studies.

claim: Inhibition of ROCK completely disrupts myosin localization and does not distinguish between myosin motor and crosslinking functions.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of ROCK, a kinase that phosphorylates the RLC, completely disrupts myosin localization and does not distinguish between myosin motor and crosslinking functions (Royou et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from prior study.

claim: Apical constriction, tissue extension, and collective cell migration defects of rock mutants or ROCK inhibition are not suppressed by expressing the RLC-EE allele.
source: Although RLC-EE enables some rock mutant flies to survive to adulthood (Winter et al., 2001), apical constriction, tissue extension, and collective cell migration defects of rock mutants or ROCK inhibition are not suppressed by expressing the RLC-EE allele, suggesting that ROCK could have other important functional targets besides myosin or that RLC-EE does not mimic the phosphorylated state (Aranjuez et al., 2016; Kasza et al., 2014; Munjal et al., 2015; Vasquez et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior studies.

claim: RLC-EE is likely forming mixed filaments with phosphorylated wild-type RLC-TS when expressed in a background where wild-type RLC-TS is also present.
source: However, this result is only obtained when the RLC-EE is expressed in a background where wild-type RLC-TS is also present. Myosin molecules can form mixed filaments (i.e. hetero-oligomers) with other myosins (Beach et al., 2014). Thus, RLC-EE is likely forming mixed filaments with phosphorylated wild-type RLC-TS and recruiting the entire complex to an abnormal location to result in the excessive constriction.
evidence: Inference based on cited prior work on myosin hetero-oligomers and experimental observations.

claim: RLC-EE is incapable of contraction without ROCK.
source: Importantly, RLC-EE is incapable of contraction without ROCK (Kasza et al., 2014; Munjal et al., 2015; Vasquez et al., 2014), suggesting that the wild-type phosphorylatable RLC is responsible for excessive cellular contraction in these experiments.
evidence: Cited from prior studies.

claim: The phosphomutants RLC-AA, RLC-AE, and RLC-EE can still bind F-actin.
source: Importantly, our in vitro motility assay results demonstrate that the phosphomutants RLC-AA, RLC-AE, and RLC-EE are clearly not mimicking phosphorylation, but can still bind F-actin.
evidence: Observed from in vitro motility assay where these mutants tethered actin filaments.

claim: Myosin motor activity determines the contraction rate during apical constriction and tissue folding.
source: Given this relationship, we propose that myosin motor activity determines the contraction rate during apical constriction and tissue folding.
evidence: Proposed conclusion based on correlation between motor activity and constriction rates.

claim: Drosophila only has one gene encoding the myosin heavy chain, unlike mammals where multiple myosin paralogs are expressed from three genes.
source: One significant advantage of Drosophila over mammalian systems is that Drosophila only has one gene encoding the myosin heavy chain, unlike the case with mammals where multiple myosin paralogs are expressed from three genes (Golomb et al., 2004; Ketchum et al., 1990; Simons et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from prior studies on myosin genes.

claim: Phosphorylation of the equivalent Serine residue in mammalian striated muscle myosin only slightly modulates the enzymatic and mechanical properties of the motor.
source: For example, phosphorylation of the equivalent Serine residue in mammalian striated muscle myosin only slightly modulates the enzymatic and mechanical properties of the motor whereas in some invertebrates muscles, such as Limulus and Tarantula, phosphorylation of this site is an on/off switch as is found in mammalian non-muscle myosins (Craig et al., 1987; Morgan et al., 1976; Sellers, 1981).
evidence: Cited from prior studies on muscle myosins.

claim: In some invertebrate muscles, such as Limulus and Tarantula, phosphorylation of the RLC Serine site is an on/off switch as is found in mammalian non-muscle myosins.
source: For example, phosphorylation of the equivalent Serine residue in mammalian striated muscle myosin only slightly modulates the enzymatic and mechanical properties of the motor whereas in some invertebrates muscles, such as Limulus and Tarantula, phosphorylation of this site is an on/off switch as is found in mammalian non-muscle myosins (Craig et al., 1987; Morgan et al., 1976; Sellers, 1981).
evidence: Cited from prior studies on invertebrate muscle myosins.

claim: Recombinant Drosophila myosin is regulated in an on/off manner by RLC phosphorylation.
source: Here, we show for the first time that recombinant Drosophila myosin is regulated in an on/off manner by RLC phosphorylation.
evidence: Demonstrated by biochemical assays showing dramatic activation upon phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of the RLC at Threonine-20 or Serine-21 activates myosin motor activity in addition to promoting the formation of bipolar filaments composed of 12.8 myosins under physiological conditions in vitro.
source: Phosphorylation of the RLC at Threonine-20 or Serine-21 activates myosin motor activity in addition to promoting the formation of bipolar filaments composed of 12.8 myosins under physiological conditions in vitro.
evidence: Demonstrated by biochemical assays and electron microscopy.

claim: RLC phosphorylation at Threonine-20 results in different mechanoenzymatic properties than phosphorylation at Serine-21.
source: Our study also shows that RLC phosphorylation at Threonine-20 results in different mechanoenzymatic properties than phosphorylation at Serine-21, in agreement with Serine-21 being the primary phosphorylation site (Bresnick et al., 1995).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing activities of RLC-TA and RLC-AS mutants.

claim: The similarity in regulatory properties between Drosophila myosin and vertebrate myosins qualifies Drosophila as an excellent model organism to study myosin function and regulation.
source: The similarity in regulatory properties between Drosophila myosin and vertebrate myosins qualifies Drosophila as an excellent model organism to study the underlying principles of myosin function and regulation in complex processes such as cell contraction and tissue folding.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of Drosophila and vertebrate myosin properties.

claim: Mutation of both Threonine-20 and Serine-21 to Alanines results in a myosin with properties similar to that of unphosphorylated mammalian myosin.
source: Mutation of both Threonine-20 and Serine-21 to Alanines results in a myosin with properties similar to that of unphosphorylated mammalian myosin; the ATPase activity is low, there is no detectable movement of actin filaments in the in vitro motility assay and the myosin does not form filaments in the presence of ATP.
evidence: Summary of RLC-AA properties from biochemical assays.

claim: Substitution of phosphorylation sites of Drosophila RLC with negatively charged residues (RLC-AE and RLC-EE) does not fully mimic the effects of phosphorylation.
source: In contrast and consistent with interpretations of past in vitro studies of smooth muscle myosin, we systematically show that substitution of phosphorylation sites of Drosophila RLC with negatively charged residues (RLC-AE and RLC-EE) does not fully mimic the effects of phosphorylation of Serine-21 and Threonine-20 with respect to both the enzymatic and motile properties of the myosin (Bresnick et al., 1995; Espinoza-Fonseca et al., 2014; Kamisoyama et al., 1994; Sweeney et al., 1994).
evidence: Demonstrated by biochemical assays and cited prior studies on smooth muscle myosin.

claim: RLC-AE and RLC-EE mutations uncouple myosin activity from regulation by upstream kinases in vivo and in vitro.
source: In addition, these mutants do not exhibit stable filament formation in vitro in the presence of ATP as occurs with phosphorylated wild type myosin. Furthermore these mutations would uncouple myosin activity from regulation by upstream kinases in vivo and in vitro (Table 2) (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated by inability of MLCK to phosphorylate these mutants.

claim: The inadequacy of acidic residues to mimic phosphorylation is most likely due to substantial chemical differences between the phosphorylated amino acid side chain and the surrogate side chain.
source: This inadequacy is most likely due to substantial chemical differences between the phosphorylated amino acid side chain and the surrogate side chain, including size and formal charge at physiological pH.
evidence: Proposed explanation based on chemical properties.

claim: An allosteric communication pathway involving the RLC, the ELC and the myosin motor domain structurally requires the presence of a phosphate moiety.
source: Reasons for the inability of negatively charged amino acids to recapitulate the phosphorylated RLC state include an allosteric communication pathway that involves the RLC, the ELC and the myosin motor domain and structurally requires the presence of a phosphate moiety (Espinoza-Fonseca et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior molecular dynamics simulation study.

claim: Mutant RLCs in which Aspartate is used as a replacement to mimic phosphorylation would also fail to faithfully mimic the phosphorylated RLC state.
source: The results from the Glutamate replacements (RLC-AE and RLC-EE) in the current study together with results from recent molecular dynamic simulation study (Espinoza-Fonseca et al., 2014) lead us to hypothesize that mutant RLCs in which Aspartate is used as a replacement to mimic phosphorylation would also fail to faithfully mimic the phosphorylated RLC state (Espinoza-Fonseca et al., 2014; Kamisoyama et al., 1994; Tang et al., 2011).
evidence: Hypothesis based on current results and cited prior studies.

claim: Caution should be used when interpreting the phenotype of so-called phosphomimetic RLC mutants in Drosophila and mammalian systems.
source: Taken together, our in vitro and in vivo data strongly suggests that caution should be used when interpreting the phenotype of so-called phosphomimetic RLC mutants in Drosophila and mammalian systems.
evidence: Recommendation based on findings that phosphomimetic mutants don't fully mimic phosphorylation.

claim: RLC phosphomutants define an allelic series that can be used to test the function of myosin motor activity in morphogenetic processes in Drosophila.
source: This study demonstrates that these RLC phosphomutants define an allelic series that can be used to test the function of myosin motor activity in morphogenetic processes in Drosophila.
evidence: Conclusion based on graded motor activity defects observed in different mutants.

claim: The RLC-AS mutant exhibited the smallest decrease in ATP hydrolysis rate at intermediate actin concentrations and also exhibited a marginal decrease in the in vivo constriction rate.
source: The RLC-AS mutant exhibited the smallest decrease in ATP hydrolysis rate at intermediate actin concentrations and also exhibited a marginal decrease in the in vivo constriction rate.
evidence: Comparison of in vitro and in vivo data for RLC-AS.

claim: Substituting an Alanine for Threonine-20 lowered the rate of actin filament sliding and had lower ATPase activity if assayed at low actin concentrations.
source: Substituting an Alanine for Threonine-20 lowered the rate of actin filament sliding and had lower ATPase activity if assayed at low actin concentrations since the Kapp for this mutant was higher than for RLC-TS.
evidence: Observed from biochemical assays of RLC-AS mutant.

claim: The RLC-AS mutation, when made in vivo, resulted in a reduced apical constriction rate, consistent with motor activity driving constriction.
source: This mutation (RLC-AS), when made in vivo also resulted in a reduced apical constriction rate, consistent with motor activity driving constriction.
evidence: Observed from time-lapse imaging of RLC-AS embryos.

claim: The RLC-TA mutant exhibited an intermediate defect in both in vitro and measured in vivo activities.
